core: Working definition of emerging adulthood: the developmental period from about age 18 to the late twenties (ages 18-29), attributed to Arnett
Why the stage is new: since about 1960, demographic trends — longer education, later marriage and parenthood — changed the timing of adult roles
Arnett's five features: identity explorations, instability, self-focus, feeling in-between, possibilities
Honest note: not everyone experiences emerging adulthood the same way; experience varies with socioeconomic circumstances
Cultural caveat: emerging adulthood is a stage of some societies, not all
Honest framing: emerging adulthood as the runway before takeoff
supporting: Legal adult statuses (vote, drive, drink, marry) arrive before settled adult roles
Median age at first marriage in the United States as an indicator of delayed adult roles
Many countries recognize a buffer period before full adulthood
outOfScope: Identity development in depth (Marcia's statuses, Erikson) — owned by the identity topic
Physical, cognitive, and sexual development in early adulthood — owned by the early-adulthood topic
Life-course sociology (cohort analysis, life-course theory) — owned by the sociology subject

claims.claim: Emerging adulthood is the developmental period from about age 18 to the late twenties — researchers commonly write ages 18 to 29 — now widely known in developmental psychology as a distinct life stage.

Emerging adulthood is the first phase of early adulthood: individuals are in the process of becoming an adult and establishing a fully adult life, holding new legal statuses (voting, driving, drinking, marrying) while a fully adult life is not yet established.

The stage is historically new: since about 1960, demographic trends toward longer time in education and later entry into marriage and parenthood created a stretch of years that earlier generations did not have as a distinct phase.
In the United States, the median age at first marriage rose from about 21 for women and 23 for men in 1970 to the late twenties for women and about 30 for men by the 2020s.
Arnett's five features of emerging adulthood are identity explorations, instability, self-focus, feeling in-between, and possibilities (an age of possibilities).

People seem to experience emerging adulthood regardless of socioeconomic status, but differently: those with fewer economic resources often have less room for identity exploration and less reason to feel optimistic about possibilities, and may delay or skip milestones such as moving out.

Emerging adulthood is a stage of some societies, not all: it took shape in post-industrial, high-income societies, and some transitions associated with early adulthood may not apply to all cultures; the experiences of people in this age range vary significantly.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is emerging adulthood a universal developmental stage or a culture-specific one?
positions: Arnett's account emphasizes that the stage took shape in societies that allow a prolonged period of independent role exploration — post-industrial, high-income societies.

The OpenStax textbook reports that people seem to experience emerging adulthood regardless of SES, but differently, and that some transitions associated with early adulthood may not apply to all cultures.
Arnett and colleagues (2014) discuss the stage's features across high-income countries with regional variation (USA, Europe, Japan).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the stage as real but variable: a working definition (about 18 to the late twenties) with five typical features, plus explicit caveats that experience differs by circumstances and that the stage is not universal.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What age range defines emerging adulthood?
positions: Arnett's original formulation (2000) emphasized the late teens through the mid-twenties.
Arnett and colleagues' later work (2014) defines the new life stage as ages 18-29.
The OpenStax textbook treats it as the first phase of early adulthood without a rigid cutoff.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the later, widely cited range — 'from about age 18 to the late twenties' (18-29) — and avoids any claim of an exact endpoint.

unsupportedExistingClaims: Draft's 'College courses use emerging adulthood as a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions' — generic boilerplate with no source support.
Draft's vocabulary definition 'A foundational Human Development concept covered in this lesson' — circular and content-free.
Draft's analogy 'Like reading a map legend before choosing a route' — generic and not specific to emerging adulthood.

sourceRecords.title: Lifespan Development, Section 11.1: Becoming an Adult
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read live at the canonical openstax.org URL (HTTP 200, full section text extracted). Supports: the working definition of emerging adulthood as the first phase of early adulthood (the process of becoming an adult; new legal statuses such as voting, driving, drinking, marrying; intense exploration of career options, beliefs, and relationships); Arnett's five features — identity exploration, instability, self-focus, feeling in-between, and being in an age of possibilities; variation by socioeconomic status (experienced regardless of SES but differently; less room for exploration and less optimism with fewer resources); the cultural caveat (some transitions of early adulthood do not apply to all cultures; experiences in this age range vary significantly); and the buffer-period framing recognized in many countries. Facts synthesized in original wording; no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The new life stage of emerging adulthood at ages 18-29 years: implications for mental health

Supports: the definition of emerging adulthood as a new life stage at ages 18-29; the demographic drivers since 1960 (longer time in education, later entry into marriage and parenthood); and discussion of the stage's features in high-income countries with regional variation (USA, Europe, Japan).
